title: Capitalization
blurb: Capitalize proper nouns, titles before names, regions, languages and the major words of titles, and leave common nouns lowercase.
question: An application essay says, “Last Spring, my Mom and i drove North to visit Mercy hospital, where doctor Ruiz taught me basic Biology.” Which words need a capital letter, which should lose one, and how do you decide?

teach.body: Formally, capital letters mark the first word of a sentence, the pronoun I, and proper nouns: the official names of specific people, places, organizations, events and works. Common nouns, which name a general type, stay lowercase. Plain English: if the word is the actual name of one particular thing (Lake Michigan, Professor Kim, Thanksgiving), capitalize it; if it describes a kind of thing (a lake, the professor, the holidays), do not.

rows: Ana Patel, Main Street, Lake Michigan
teach.caption: Capitalize the first word of a quoted full sentence too: She said, “Wash your hands.”

teach.caption: A language is always capitalized, even as a subject. Other subjects are capitalized only as a numbered course name.

teach.body: Gabriela Flores, a nursing applicant, revises: “Last spring, my mom and I drove north to visit Mercy Hospital, where Doctor Ruiz taught me basic biology.” Spring is a season: lowercase. My mom has a possessive: lowercase. I is always a capital. North is a direction to drive, not a region: lowercase. Mercy Hospital is the full name of one hospital: both words capitalized. Doctor comes before a name: capitalized. Biology is a general subject: lowercase.

items: Find each capitalized word and ask: is it a specific name, or a general word?
Check titles and family words: before a name or used as a name gets a capital; after my/the does not.
Check directions (region or movement?), seasons (lowercase) and subjects (language or course number?).
Check lowercase words that should be capitals: I, languages, holidays, first word of a quote.

teach.text: The HESI A2 traps run both ways: capitalizing seasons (“Fall”), general subjects (“Chemistry” in “I study chemistry”), directions (“drove South”) or “doctor” with no name, and NOT capitalizing a title before a name (“doctor Patel”), a language (“english”), or a region (“the midwest”).

items: Capitalize proper nouns: specific people, places, organizations, days, months, holidays, events, documents.
Lowercase seasons, general subjects and compass directions; capitalize languages and regions.
Titles and family words are capitalized only before a name or when used as a name.
In titles of works, capitalize first, last and major words; lowercase short articles, conjunctions and prepositions.
Capitalize the pronoun I and the first word of a quoted full sentence.

summary: You can now capitalize proper nouns, titles before names, regions, languages, events and the major words of titles, while keeping seasons, subjects, directions and general titles lowercase. You can also check every word in an option, because capitalization errors on the HESI A2 can run in either direction.

options: We start classes in the Fall, after Labor Day.
We start classes in the fall, after labor day.
We start classes in the Fall, after labor Day.
We start classes in the fall, after Labor Day.
A.why: Seasons are lowercase; the name of a holiday is capitalized.

whyNot.0: Fall is a season, so it is lowercase.
whyNot.1: Labor Day is the name of a holiday, so both words are capitalized.
whyNot.2: Fall should be lowercase, and both words of Labor Day need capitals.

A.q: Which sentence capitalizes the titles correctly?
options: Yesterday, Doctor Patel met the director of nursing.
Yesterday, doctor Patel met the director of nursing.
Yesterday, Doctor Patel met the Director Of Nursing.
Yesterday, doctor Patel met the Director of nursing.
A.why: A title directly before a name is capitalized; a title used generally (the director of nursing) is not.

whyNot.1: Doctor comes directly before the name Patel, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.2: “The director of nursing” is a general title with no name, and “of” would never be capitalized.
whyNot.3: Doctor needs a capital before the name, and the general title needs none.

A.q: Which sentence capitalizes the region and the direction correctly?
options: After living in the midwest, Kayla drove south to Texas.
After living in the Midwest, Kayla drove South to Texas.
After living in the Midwest, Kayla drove south to Texas.
After living in the midwest, Kayla drove South to texas.
A.why: The Midwest names a region (capitalized); “drove south” is a direction of travel (lowercase).

whyNot.0: The Midwest is the name of a region, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.1: “Drove south” gives a direction, not a region, so south is lowercase.
whyNot.3: This reverses both rules and also lowercases the state name Texas.

B.q: Which sentence capitalizes the family words correctly?
options: I asked mom if my Grandma could visit.
I asked Mom if my grandma could visit.
I asked Mom if my Grandma could visit.
I asked mom if my grandma could visit.
B.why: Mom is used as a name (capital); “my grandma” follows a possessive (lowercase).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: Mom is used as a name, and “my grandma” is not.
whyNot.2: After the possessive “my,” grandma is lowercase.
whyNot.3: Mom is used in place of her name here, so it is capitalized.

B.q: Which sentence capitalizes the school subjects correctly?
options: Nadia is taking Biology, english, and Chemistry 110.
Nadia is taking biology, english, and chemistry 110.
Nadia is taking biology, English, and Chemistry 110.
Nadia is taking Biology, English, and chemistry 110.
B.why: General subjects are lowercase (biology), languages are always capitalized (English), and a numbered course name is capitalized (Chemistry 110).

whyNot.0: Biology is a general subject (lowercase), and English is a language (always capitalized).
whyNot.1: English is a language, and Chemistry 110 is a specific course name; both need capitals.
whyNot.3: Biology is general, so lowercase; Chemistry 110 is a course name, so capitalized.

B.q: Which sentence about a history class is capitalized correctly?
options: In history class, we studied the Civil War and the Constitution.
In History class, we studied the Civil War and the Constitution.
In history class, we studied the civil war and the Constitution.
In history class, we studied the Civil War and the constitution.
B.why: History is a general subject (lowercase); historical events and documents (the Civil War, the Constitution) are capitalized.

whyNot.1: History is a general subject, not a numbered course or a language, so it is lowercase.
whyNot.2: The Civil War names a specific historical event, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.3: The Constitution names a specific historical document, so it is capitalized.

C.q: Which book title is capitalized correctly?
options: A Guide To Caring For The Heart
A guide to caring for the heart
a Guide to Caring for the Heart
A Guide to Caring for the Heart
C.why: Capitalize the first word and the major words; lowercase short prepositions (to, for) and articles (the) in the middle.

whyNot.0: Short prepositions and articles in the middle of a title stay lowercase.
whyNot.1: Major words such as Guide, Caring and Heart must be capitalized.
whyNot.2: The first word of a title is always capitalized.

C.q: Which sentence capitalizes the quotation correctly?
options: The nurse said, “wash your hands before you enter.”
The nurse said, “Wash your hands before you enter.”
The Nurse said, “Wash your hands before you enter.”
the nurse said, “Wash your hands before you enter.”
C.why: The first word of a sentence and the first word of a quoted full sentence are capitalized.

whyNot.0: A quoted full sentence starts with a capital letter.
whyNot.2: “The nurse” is a general noun, not a title before a name.
whyNot.3: The first word of the sentence must be capitalized.

C.q: Gabriela's essay says, “Last Spring, i volunteered at Mercy hospital with professor Kim.” Which revision is correct?
options: Last spring, I volunteered at Mercy hospital with Professor Kim.
Last Spring, I volunteered at Mercy Hospital with Professor Kim.
Last spring, I volunteered at Mercy Hospital with Professor Kim.
Last spring, I volunteered at Mercy Hospital with professor Kim.
C.why: Seasons are lowercase, I is always capitalized, the full name Mercy Hospital is capitalized, and a title before a name is capitalized.

whyNot.0: Hospital is part of the proper name Mercy Hospital, so it needs a capital.
whyNot.1: Spring is a season, so it is lowercase.
whyNot.3: Professor comes directly before the name Kim, so it is capitalized.

reteach.title: Capitals are name badges
reteach.question: Imagine only specific, named things are allowed to wear a badge with a capital letter. Who gets a badge, and who has to give theirs back?

blocks.body: Professor Kim wears a badge, because it is her name and title together; “the professor” does not, because it could be anyone. Lake Michigan gets one; “the lake” does not. Thanksgiving gets one, but winter does not, because a season is not a name (unless it is part of one, as in the Winter Olympics). English always keeps its badge, because it is the name of a language, while biology only earns one inside a course name such as Biology 101.

blocks.text: A word can lose its badge in the same sentence it wore one: “Doctor Patel is the best doctor on staff.”

explain.body: Capitalize the first word of every sentence, the pronoun I, and proper nouns such as days, months, holidays, streets and specific places. Common nouns (the clinic) stay lowercase.

test.q: Which sentence about a Monday visit is capitalized correctly?
options: On Monday, I will visit the clinic on Main Street.
On monday, I will visit the clinic on Main Street.
On Monday, i will visit the clinic on Main Street.
On Monday, I will visit the Clinic on Main street.
test.why: Days, the pronoun I and street names are capitalized; the general noun clinic is not.

whyNot.1: Days of the week are capitalized: Monday.
whyNot.2: The pronoun I is always capitalized.
whyNot.3: Clinic is a common noun, and Street is part of the name Main Street.

explain.body: Capitalize a title directly before a name (Senator Ortiz). Lowercase it when it stands alone or follows the name (Ana Patel, the director).

rows.label: Example
values: the senator; Ana Patel, the director

test.q: Which sentence capitalizes the titles of people correctly?
options: Ana Patel, the Director, thanked Senator Ortiz.
Ana Patel, the director, thanked senator Ortiz.
Ana Patel, The director, thanked Senator Ortiz.
Ana Patel, the director, thanked Senator Ortiz.
test.why: “The director” follows the name, so it is lowercase; Senator comes before a name, so it is capitalized.

whyNot.0: A title after a name is lowercase.
whyNot.1: Senator comes directly before the name Ortiz, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.2: “The” in the middle of a sentence is lowercase.

explain.body: Languages and nationalities are always capitalized (English, Spanish). Compass words are capitalized only when they name a region (the West, the Midwest), not when they give a direction (drive west).

test.q: Which sentence about the English teacher is capitalized correctly?
options: Our english teacher grew up in the West.
Our English teacher grew up in the West.
Our English teacher grew up in the west.
Our English Teacher grew up in the West.
test.why: English is a language (capital), teacher is a common noun (lowercase), and the West names a region (capital).

whyNot.0: English is the name of a language, so it is always capitalized.
whyNot.2: “The West” names a region where she grew up, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.3: Teacher is a common noun, not a title before a name.

explain.h: Events, holidays and titles of works
explain.body: Capitalize historical events and documents (the Civil War) and holidays (Thanksgiving). In titles of works, capitalize the first, last and major words.

test.q: Which sentence capitalizes the event and the holiday correctly?
options: We read about the Civil War over Thanksgiving break.
We read about the civil war over Thanksgiving break.
We read about the Civil War over thanksgiving break.
We read about the Civil war over Thanksgiving Break.
test.why: The Civil War is a named historical event and Thanksgiving is a holiday; “break” is a common noun.

whyNot.1: The Civil War names a specific event, so both words are capitalized.
whyNot.2: Thanksgiving is the name of a holiday, so it is capitalized.
whyNot.3: War is part of the event's name, and break is a common noun.
